utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-08-91-T. The Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. Before the witness is escorted back to the stand, there is a ruling that we have to deliver. May I have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Matthew Olmsted, Joanna Korner, and Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, and Eugene O'Sullivan for Stanisic Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For Zupljanin Defence, Igor Pantelic and Dragan Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 18th of May, the Trial Chamber admitted into evidence pursuant to Rule 92 ter, two witness statements of Ian Traynor, but denied admission of 15 articles that formed part of his Rule 92 ter package. On the 21st of May, the Prosecutor requested the Trial Chamber to reconsider the admission into evidence of "at least the specific articles that Ms. Pidwell asked Mr. Traynor about," during his testimony on the 17th and 18th of May. It is recalled that the Trial Chamber has discretionary power to reconsider a previous decision if a clear error of reasoning has been demonstrated or if it's necessary to do so to prevent injustice. On the 2nd of October, 2009, the Trial Chamber issued a decision pursuant to Rule 92 ter which concerned several witnesses including Traynor. In that decision, after reviewing the documents accompanying the witness's prior evidence, the Trial Chamber had held that in keeping with the jurisprudence -- "in keeping with the jurisprudence of the Tribunal, the Trial Chamber will, when admitting into evidence the prior transcript and written statements of the witness pursuant to Article 92 ter also admit all the accompanying documents save those identified for the reasons that it views this evidence as an integral whole." While ruling orally on the 18th May, the Trial Chamber did not take into consideration this prior ruling and had no intention to modify or overrule the prior decision that it erroneously [indiscernible]. This amounts to a clear error of reasoning since it affects the parties' legitimate expectations with regard to the consequences of the prior ruling. Having considered the oral submissions on this matter of the Prosecution and the Defence, the Trial Chamber by majority with Judge Harhoff dissenting decides, therefore, to reconsider its oral decision dated 18 May 2010. It, therefore, holds that in accordance with the 2nd of October decision and for the reason stated therein, consequence upon the admission into evidence of the written statement of Ian Traynor pursuant to Article 92 ter, the 15 accompanying articles included in the 92 ter package are also admissible. The Trial Chamber, thus, admits the 15 articles as 92 ter evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you Judge Delvoie. Judge Harhoff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I respectfully disagree with the Trial Chamber's decision to admit into evidence all of the 15 articles originally identified by the Prosecution as being "indispensable and inextricable." Documents accompanying the statements of witness Ian Traynor. The Trial Chamber did, indeed, admit these articles into evidence in its decision of 2nd October, 2009 in which it accepted the Prosecution's 92 ter package of this witness. In my view, however, evidentiary admission at such an early stage seven months prior to the witness's testimony in court must be read with a natural reservation that accompanying documents should ultimately not be admitted into evidence if the information that they contain has been provided meanwhile to the Trial Chamber, either by the witness's oral testimony or through other evidence. The Trial Chamber's admission into evidence of the 15 articles back in October 2009, thus, was only and could only have been of a provisional nature. It goes for all earlier statements and testimonies of witnesses who are called under Rule 92 ter of the rules that these statements or testimonies are only admitted into evidence by the end of the witness's testimony, and it would indeed seem peculiar if the accompanying documents were to be admitted separately from and prior to the previous statements and testimonies. An accompanying document should only be admitted into evidence along with the witness's earlier statement or testimony to the extent in which they are still considered to form an indispensable and inextricable part of the statement or the early testimony by the end of the witness's testimony in the present case. If, in contrast, evidence has been offered which enables the Trial Chamber to fully appreciate the contents of the witness's written statement or earlier testimony, then there is no longer any need for admitting the accompanying documents into evidence for the reason that they form an indispensable and inextricable part of the statement or the testimony. This view also finds support in the Tribunal's judicial practice, and I refer to the decision of 3rd November, 2009, in Tolimir, and it was at paragraph 7 of that decision. In the present instance, I am of the view that all of the relevant parts of the information contained in the 15 articles in relation to the two statements had been elicited directly from the witness during his testimony and through the videos that were shown to him. None of the 15 articles appear to me to include information without which the witness's statements cannot be fully understood, and the Prosecution does not, therefore, suffer any prejudice from being prevented from entering these 15 articles into evidence through this witness. I am, accordingly, of the view that the Trial Chamber's ruling on 18th May, 2010, was correct and should stand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. There's one other matter before the witness comes in. The -- we are in receipt of a motion for -- further motion for protective measures in respect of, as I recall, three witnesses, two of whom are scheduled to appear within the next fortnight or so and because of the nearness of the schedule date of testimony of those witnesses, we will respectfully invite expedited responses from the Defence in respect of that application. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, can we do it on Monday?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, I was going to say by the end of the week forgetting that Friday is a non-sitting day, but Monday would be fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, could the witness be escorted back to the stand, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Radulovic, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: For what I trust will be the last time in this appearance of yours before the Tribunal, I remind you you are still on your oath. Yes, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Radulovic.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: At the end of the session yesterday, you were testifying about the reaction of the SDB leadership at the RS MUP level to the information contained in your intelligence reports. I need to clarify a couple of things for the record. First, you testified that the information in your reports about crimes against a non-Serb population did not earn the interest of the Republika Srpska leadership. Are you referring to the RS leadership in general or the SDB leadership?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was referring exclusively to the leadership of the state security service or National Security Service. I have later seen that many of my reports never reached the political leadership, not even the leadership at the level of the Security Services Centre or MUP of Republika Srpska, which goes to show that most of the reports remain in the desks of my immediate superior and his immediate superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Second clarification, can you give us some examples of the crimes against non-Serb population that the SDB leadership at the RS MUP level attempted to minimise in 1992?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, everything that took place in the municipality of Prijedor, I will not now enumerate all the different location, although I can, then again there were attempts to minimise what was going on in the area of Banja Luka. Some prominent figures from Banja Luka were killed, some people were taken away and were never found. Again not even their remains have been found up until today. Please don't misunderstand me, such cases happened in almost all municipalities, Kotor Varos, Doboj, all the other municipalities we reported about. But we also wrote about crimes that Bosniaks and Croats committed against Serbian population. I have seen none of such reports of that kind here in your documents, but a similar situation existed in Zenica and other areas we reported about.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You testified in relation to the killings at Koricanske Stene that you provided the minister of interior information about the events surrounding these killings through Zivko Bojic. Do you recall whether there are other instances you provided Mr. Bojic with information about crimes against non-Serbs to relay it up to the minister?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I told you already that I tried to provide as much information about crimes committed in the area of Republika Srpska to Mr. Zivko Bojic. Mr. Bojic and Mr. Branko Ratic, both of them, and I believe that the second gentleman, with thanks to his friendship with the minister of the interior, namely they went to high school together or were rather the same age and, therefore, I believe that some or most of the information would be forwarded in the form I gave to him. What of this he managed to forward, that, I don't know. But what I do know is that in relation to the Koricanske Stene incident, there was a response by the minister of the interior. I've seen a circular dispatch that was sent asking to take all the necessary measures to clarify this incident, to bring in the persons who committed this crime, interviewing them and furthering on the process. That's not the only topic I discussed with Mr. Zivko Bojic. I discussed some other cases with him and with Branko Ratic. Some of these cases I still remember, and some I may have forgotten.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What about the camps, the detention facilities and camps in Prijedor, is that a topic that you discussed with Mr. Bojic to relay up to the ministry?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Sir, I know that I had conversations with Zivko Bojic about that, and I must add also with Branko Ratic. Now, what form and to what extent I may have talked about it, I cannot remember at the moment, but it couldn't have been less than what was contained in written reports to my superiors. Sir, let me be even more specific. I also discussed with Mr. Zivko Bojic some members of the special detachment of whom we have heard and had information about that they were committing crimes. Again I do not know how much of that Zivko Bojic may have used in his further work or in transferring the information forwarding them to others. I had and still have unlimited trust and confidence in expertise and honesty of Mr. Zivko Bojic. That's all I can say about this topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what about Vladimir Tutus, was he also, to your knowledge, relaying information about crimes against non-Serbs up to the minister?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, object. I don't think that Vladimir Tutus was ever mentioned during the cross-examination, Your Honours. Ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, that doesn't matter. This is going to information getting up to the RS MUP level, which was thoroughly addressed during cross-examination. And this is just one other avenue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, there was no -- there was no evidence on direct about Vladimir Tutus at all. So if Mr. Olmsted is saying that this was another avenue, he should have explored that during the direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic has put in another way the question I was about to ask, Mr. Olmsted. What is the -- you are in re-examination now, I remind you. What is the -- why the specifics about this particular individual, which as Mr. Zecevic has said, wasn't raised in examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This wasn't raised in examination-in-chief because the issue of information not making its way up the chain of command was not an issue during examination. It became an issue during cross-examination. And so the Prosecution is exploring ways in which information, even alternative ways, that information made it up to the RS MUP level, and this is just one other example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, perhaps you may achieve your end by rephrasing the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You mentioned Zivko Bojic and also Mr. I believe it's Ratic, who was providing information up to the minister. Was there anyone else in the public security service who was also providing information regarding crimes against non-Serbs up the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Sir, I never stated that Ratic forwarded information to the minister of the interior. Mr. Ratic was directly linked up with the organs of the military security and Radovan Karadzic and, therefore, I know for a fact that he was not a very good friend of the Ministry of the Interior and the minister himself. The Ministry of the Interior had had some complaints concerning his work and he, in turn, avoided contacts with the public security service, precisely because of the fact that he knew that the ministry wanted to put under its control some of his activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That's fine, Mr. Radulovic. Let's get to my question, though, which is, if it's not Mr. Ratic, that's fine. Other than Zivko Bojic was there anyone else in the public security sector who was relaying information up the chain of command regarding crimes against non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, let me be specific. I know that most often I talked about crimes against non-Serbs with Zivko Bojic from public security, sometimes with Mr. Vladimir Tutus, and this is where my knowledge about that ends, knowledge about whether they did or -- as for that knowledge, I don't know whether they passed that on or not. I really cannot say. All I can say is that in terms of certain events, I saw that the MUP was reacting. I don't know if this is because Zivko Bojic or Vladimir Tutus or Slobodan [as interpreted] Zupljanin informed about that to the ministry. This is something I really cannot say anything about.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: But they came to you, is it correct, they came to you to gather information to relay up there, whether they did or not, that is a different matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm really sorry. Can we have the reference for this?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is again going to communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm really sorry, Your Honours, but this is misinterpretation of the whole testimony of the witness. I never heard the witness saying this at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: In any event, Mr. Olmsted, I think you've made your point. Let's go. Because the witness has explained that he received this information, he is aware that there were certain actions on the part of the MUP, but he doesn't really know what happened afterwards. Let's move on. I should say, he is not in a position to testify affirmatively as to what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: But my question, of course, is not geared to whether it actually got there but the purpose of them coming to him for information was to relay it up. Whether they did, in fact, is a different matter. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'll move on. I want to briefly clarify --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, sorry, just one qualification for the transcript, because on page 10, line 6, it was recorded Slobodan Zupljanin, witness said Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, Mr. Prosecutor. The contacts between me and Zivko Bojic were direct contacts, and we didn't have any obligation towards each other to go to each other. We met practically every day in the building. He worked on the fourth floor -- on the second floor, and I worked on the fourth floor and because we were friends and colleagues, and I had a lot of respect for him. Because of that in our communication, I would share what I saw, noticed, heard. I never provided him with any kind of written trail, and he didn't provide me with that either. I would like to be very precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That's fine. We are going to move on to another topic. I want to briefly clarify a few matters concerning your 1999 encounter with Mico Stanisic at the intercontinental hotel. This is at page 11016 of the transcript. Did Mr. Stanisic claim that he had not seen any of your intelligence teams report or just not all of them?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: First let me correct myself. Later when I thought back about that, it was after the death or the killing of Zeljko Raznjatovic, and this was in 2000, not in 1999, and I remember well that it was a cold winter period. I don't need to speak about all the particulars that I remember, they are not that important, but what is important is that this was my first direct contact, meeting with Mr. Mico Stanisic who is here in this courtroom and --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you there --

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Let me just, let me just -- all right, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I want to wrap this up as quickly as possible. Again, did Mr. Stanisic during this conversation claim he had not seen any of your reports or just that he had not seen all of them, that is my question?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to be very brief then. He said that most of the things that we talked about he had not been informed about. As for what that most means, that's something that he knows, but I do know that he said that he did [as interpreted] know about the majority or most of the things that we talked about. He didn't learn about them, wasn't informed about them, and that for most of those things, about most of those things he learned from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, page 12, line 13, I believe the witness said that he did not know about the majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Is that right, Mr. Radulovic, he said he did not know about the majority of things? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. It's like you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Okay. Now, do you recall based on your conversation with Mr. Stanisic what crimes against non-Serb population he had received information through intelligence channels?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, sir, this happened 11 years ago. It was a long conversation. I cannot remember all the details and the cases that we discussed, but I do remember that we touched upon almost all the cases that had been mentioned in my testimony here before this Tribunal. Of course, not in as much detail, but my impression is, my impression is that he was really insufficiently informed, to say the least.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's look at -- to refresh your recollection, why don't we look at paragraph 28 of your written statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm really sorry, Your Honours. We went through this situation with the written statement -- during the cross, this particular subject was not open. Now Mr. Olmsted wants to refresh the memory of the witness, and he didn't -- he failed to ask him this on the direct. I honestly think that this is putting the Defence in a position which is, in my opinion, unfair. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Except, Mr. Zecevic, I would have thought that this flows directly out of the -- what was dealt with in cross-examination about this meeting that the witness would have had with the accused Stanisic. It's -- and this matter of the witness even at the instance of the -- of counsel looking at his statement and then asked to -- the question again we've dealt with before. Yes, Mr. Olmsted, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Radulovic, if you can please read paragraph 28 to yourself and once you have, I'll ask you a question again.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I've read it. I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I want to focus on this conversation with Mr. Stanisic and from that conversation what you could tell that he did know, that he did learn from your intelligence information about crimes against non-Serbs. Can you tell us what you could tell that he did know, what crimes he did know about?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Sir, I have just read this carefully, and I see that I have absolutely repeated back now to you what I said then. I don't know how you understand it, but the statement reflects what I said in essence that I found out from the conversation with him that he knew about the events in Prijedor and Teslic and Doboj because these were well known cases and events which anyone who lived in Republika Srpska could have known about, so for me as an operative, I would have been very disappointed had Mico Stanisic not heard about these cases. We did speak about the cases in Prijedor, in Teslic, in Doboj, and in other places in that conversation in 2000. And we talked about those cases as occurrences without any particular analysis, how they came about, who participated, and about the consequences of these events. It was his general understanding and mine that he was not informed in a timely manner about those events, and this is what I would like to stress because I saw that the person didn't know that we had written an information about this report two days before, about the event in Brod, that he didn't know until the commission went out or later that there had been crimes in Keraterm, in Omarska, Brisevo, I don't have to list all the names. I didn't say that he did not have information that that had happened, but what I understood was that he did not have timely and complete information, and this is what I told you before, what I'm telling you now, and what in a certain way was a kind of objection to the statement because it does not reflect everything that we talked about, about certain events, Mr. Prosecutor, with you and with others, because I never actually talk about consequences without mentioning the effects [as interpreted]. I don't abbreviate anything. These are very sensitive matters about which I always try to provide my complete opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just one clarification in the transcript. Page 15, line 7, I believe the witness said, I never actually talk about the consequences without mentioning the causes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I think that's what I heard as well, but just.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Recorded the effects, that's why I went up.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Is that correct, Mr. Radulovic, just yes or no?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, yes, as Mr. Zecevic corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, could you tell, and again looking at this paragraph in your statement, could you tell that some of the information he had --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Olmsted, haven't you gone as far as you could go with this with this witness. Let's move on. You've asked a question, you've gotten an answer. Your interpretation of the document in respect of -- on which the witness's refreshed his memory is at the end of the day neither here nor there. The witness has looked at it and he has answered your question. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Are you aware how frequently Mico Stanisic travelled to Belgrade in 1992? And if you are not, just say you don't know.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I will tell you. I don't know how many times I went to Belgrade, never mind how many times the minister of Internal Affairs went there, and for what reasons. Really, you overestimate me. I'm just a person who had a relatively small number of operatives, and I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: -- with this we are really perhaps asking too much of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That's fine, and if you don't know please just say so and we'll move on. The Defence also asked you a number of questions regarding whether your reports made it to Mr. Zupljanin. On your first day of testimony, you were asked how Mr. Zupljanin received information contained in your intelligence reports, to which you responded on page 10731 "Stojan Zupljanin, the chief, received our reports and information through Vojin Bera and Nedeljko Kesic. As far as I know this was done at their expert staff meetings, but I'm not sure whether all pieces of information or the extent of the information that reached Stojan Zupljanin. I know that concerning certain events, I directly got in touch with Zupljanin." You then testified at page 10731, "all instances in which there were certain abuse of other structures, organs of the police and army, or crimes committed by these structures in addition to a written report, I always made an effort to inform Mr. Stojan Zupljanin orally as well." Which is consistent with your prior interviews. Do you stand by those answers?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. And, please, I would like it to be very clear, I mentioned six or seven cases that I recall talking about with Stojan Zupljanin whereby I want to say that I can mention those six or seven cases again, but that doesn't mean that I talked about all the cases, all the events with Stojan Zupljanin at the critical time when some events happened, I know that Stojan Zupljanin even wasn't in Banja Luka, he was busy at the front near Orasje. So I would like you to understand that my communication with Stojan Zupljanin wasn't as frequent as you think.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Were you aware whether officials from the Serbia state security contacted Mr. Zupljanin on occasion about information contained in your Milos reports?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. Marko Lazovic told me that he did talk with Stojan Zupljanin about some information that we had. Marko Lazovic is from the state security service in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You testified at several points during cross-examination that you believed that Vojin Bera was not forwarding all your information to his superiors. First, can you explain why you never raised this matter during any of your interviews with the Office of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, you never asked me, and to tell you the truth, I didn't really feel the need to impose. Sir, if I'm publicly testifying here about that, wouldn't it have been better for me to tell you something like that in a hotel room rather than here like this in public before the whole world, if I may put it that way? I told you, and you can find that in the transcript, that we avoided conflict with Vojin Bera. I don't know if this is enough because I had also indicated some other things in reference to Vojin Bera.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If I understand your testimony, you did not discover this problem with Bera not communicating information to his superiors until either late or after the armed conflict; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Which armed conflict do you mean? Sir, your question is not clear to me. I told you that -- may I answer specifically. It's a matter of truth, and I must answer. Mr. Prosecutor, sir, we -- you -- before we began our operative work as the Milos group, who behaved in what way, we knew that the number one man in the state security service at the time in Banja Luka who signed his membership to the SDS was Ivan Figurek and we knew that Vojin Bera was close to those ideas. We knew that he was egocentric, that he was a man without moral and other --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Radulovic.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Please, please. And I told you that at the beginning, and this is why we avoided him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Because I have limited time I really just want to focus on the question. We understand that Mr. Bera was a member of the SDS party. But I want to get the time-frame when you learned that Mr. Bera was not providing all your information up the chain of command. Was this contemporaneous with your reports, or did you learn this closer to 1995, 1996, that time-frame?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Later. Later. After the events we found out that they were not sending them. If I misunderstood you, I'm sorry, sir. We found out that Vojin Bera was not sending timely and complete reports of ours, and he did that only once -- or we only found out about that once the war was over, and I understood that actually from conversations I had later with Mr. Stojan Zupljanin and Mr. Mico Stanisic and why wouldn't I also say with also Jovica Stanisic after he was released the first time and came back to Belgrade as an operative. That was when I actually learned that the three of them were not receiving complete information and they were not receiving them in a timely manner. The reports that were being sent by the Milos group.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So this issue of Bera not communicating information never came up during a meeting with Mr. Kesic or Mr. Zupljanin, for instance, when you asked them whether they received one of your reports, and they responded, no, we actually never saw your report, this issue didn't come up?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, sir. It didn't even occur to me to think that somebody was holding back information and was not sending them in a regular way, the way they were written by the Milos group.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Umm --

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: And another thing, I never, I nor any of the other Milos group members ever attended a single meeting of the professional collegium at the National Security Service and the Security Services Centre, and we were never in Pale in the National Security Service or at the Pale Ministry of Internal Affairs when this problem would be discussed with anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Radulovic, is it the case, isn't it, that in 1992 you were reporting directly to Mr. Kesic and not through Mr. Bera?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct. About certain events.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, you've had an opportunity to review, as you put it, over 1.000 pages of your reports from 1992. Did any of those reports appear to have been doctored by someone?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I really couldn't say anything about that. I can say that I looked through as many pages as you gave me from 1992. I think there were some 1.200 pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And although, as you've testified, some of those reports were missing, would you agree that a significant number of them were kept at the CSB even until after the conflict when the Office of the Prosecution, this Tribunal, seised them, including a number of the reports that we've asked questions about during this trial?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can agree with this assertion of yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I want to move on to a different topic now. I want to ask some questions about the scenario you testified about on cross-examination by which non-Serb civilians moved out of towns with mixed ethnicities immediately prior to the shelling of those towns by non-Serb armed forces. First, just to clarify, I apologise if I've misunderstood your testimony, but is it your position that non-Serbs left the mixed towns under Bosnian Serb control solely in order to permit non-Serb forces to shell those towns?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, it's the other way around. You've stated it the other way around. The Muslims and the Croats had moved so that those areas could be shelled from Bosanski Brod, Teslic, I mentioned some places, I could refer to some other places as well. What I'm saying is that the Croats were going to places where they lived together with the Serbs and after that there would be shelling either from Croatia or from parts under the control of the Croats. The same thing would happen when we are talking about Bosniaks. There were also some Serbs who had been detained because it was assumed that they were guiding directly the shells of the Croat armed forces and those of the Bosniak side who had arrived before that as refugees to the side that was under the control of the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, maybe you misunderstood my question. I understand the scenario you have given us, but my question is with regard to motive. Were non-Serbs leaving these municipalities solely to allow non-Serb forces to shell those mixed towns, or did they have other reasons to leave those mixed towns?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, if you move members of your ethnic group out of an area, then you can fire without discrimination. You can fire wherever you want, wherever it lands, the shell, you've achieved something, you've destroyed something that belongs to the enemy side.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I think you are still misunderstanding my question. Perhaps I could show you a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could see P1399 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, it's P1399.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Can you give us a tab number, Mr. Olmsted?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I think it's -- I have to look back at my old notes. I think it's tab 33. So it's 65 ter 2837. I believe this was on -- it's been admitted previously. I'm sorry, it's P1345. That's my mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is a report -- Milos report dated 11 July 1992. This report discusses two currents in SDS in the Doboj region as well as in certain municipalities in the Bosanska Krajina. One is more moderate while the other is -- while the other "was developing the idea of ethnically cleansed environments and did not hesitate to resort to whatever means necessary to attain this goal." Can you tell us in which municipalities in Northern Bosnia and Bosanska Krajina the second current of the SDS was manifesting itself?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can list you the municipalities where this was a prominent case instead of telling you that -- basing this on geographical locations. Prijedor, Doboj, Teslic, Kljuc, Sanski Most. Do you need any other?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What about Prijedor? Yes, you mentioned Prijedor, I'm sorry. I've been distracted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now I'm told that it's P1388. I think we have the right B/C/S version up here, but the English version is incorrect for some reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Radulovic, you use the term "ethnic cleansing." What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Listen, I know how one should define that from the theory point of view, but I will tell you how I understand it. Members of one people or one religious or ethnic group is being driven from one territory to another territory exclusively because they belong to a certain religious or ethnic group.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, with regard to Teslic, you mentioned during your testimony that, on examination, that there were no major armed conflicts in this municipality before the Mice group arrived in the municipality. So can you tell us when in 1992 did the non-Serb forces shell Teslic town?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Throughout 1992 from two different locations. One location was from the area of Tesanj because the border-line dividing Teslic and Tesanj is rather long. And the other location was the area of Slatine and Komusina. There was daily shelling from there. The only population there was a group of about 10.000 Croats who were linked up with Zepca. They were getting their logistics from Zepce and they shelled Banja Vrucica and the town of Teslic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May I focus my question. You mentioned that this occurred in 1992, this shelling of Teslic town. I just want to focus on the mixed town of Teslic. Can you give us a month in 1992 where you say this shelling occurred, just so we have a time-frame, or at least a series of months?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: So June, July for sure. And as for other times of shelling, I cannot comment that because I was not present in the area of Teslic at the time. Now, in relation to the shelling that took place in June and July, one can find records of on-site investigations because in some of the shellings there were casualties, people got killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Is it possible that non-Serbs were leaving Teslic town because of the Mice group's activities in that town?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: With regard to Doboj town, we are just focusing on the town, not the municipality, did the shelling of that town by non-Serb forces occur before or after the Serb take-over of that town?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: After the take-over, not before the take-over. Once the Serbs took over the power in town, I can put this differently, but I think this is clear enough, there was frequent shelling from the area under the control of the Bosniak army not far away from the town itself. The centre of the Doboj town was about 2 and a half kilometres away from the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And that's fine, I'm not asking for details about the actual shelling, I'm just asking some general questions about it. Is it possible, Mr. Radulovic, that the arrival of the Red Berets and the Banja Luka Special Police detachment was what motivated non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, aren't you asking the witness for a conclusion? At the end of the day you can put this in your final submission and it is would be for the Chamber, but -- and while I've interrupted you, we require you to wrap up your cross-examination [sic] by 10.25.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Very well, I'm going to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Banja Luka town, was that shelled by non-Serb forces in 1992?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I don't have information about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: In 1992 did non-Serb forces shell Sanski Most town?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm not informed about that, but I do think they may have.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: In 1992, did non-Serb forces shell Kotor Varos town, not the municipality -- elsewhere in the municipality, just the town?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There were exchanges of artillery fire from Vecici, from Vecici against the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Was the primary reason that the non-Serb population left Kotor Varos town was to permit -- was this to permit this shelling, or were they leaving for other reasons based on your intelligence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: That's a conclusion, isn't it, again?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, this is all with regard to this issue of whether --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It's not cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, it's re-examination, and this issue came up during cross-examination. Your Honours asked some questions about it, and we are seeking to clarify where this scenario occurred of non-Serbs leaving the municipality immediately prior to non-Serb shelling in order to permit the destruction of the town with only Serbs in it, and we have to get this parameter down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: This "in order to permit" is where it seems to be the problem lies in your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Very well, I'm going to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I want to talk just briefly about the town commands. In the municipalities that had these town commands, were the SJB chiefs members of those commands?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: If you are talking about town commands, each and every chief of SJB was part of the town command but it was under the town command. The chief of the police station had to report to the town command and was resubordinated, that's the proper term, to the town command.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, in these municipalities, the town commander or a representative from the town command was on the Crisis Staff, isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And wasn't the purpose of these town commands to co-ordinate the activities of Serb armed forces in municipalities where there was a garrison and, therefore, a number of overlapping armed forces --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... isn't that the purpose? We're presenting our case, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: It sounds as if you are giving evidence, Mr. Olmsted. Ask the question again. Please rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'll as the question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Wasn't the role of these town commands a co-ordinating function?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It is the same, ask him directly, what was the purpose of the town command. Of course, if he knows.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What was their purpose then?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I must say that I feel more and more that I'm becoming an expert of a sort, but because I happen to know this, I can give you an answer. I have a lot of respect for you and the Trial Chamber. The town commands was in charge of establishing local armed formations for the defence of the territory that belonged to the town. In other words, they were using both members of the army as well as the members of the active and reserve staff of the police to form these units. The town commander was entitled to use and mobilise reserve and active elements of the police and send them to perform activities and tasks without asking either the ministry or the CSB without, in other words, having even to ask either the chief of the CSB or the minister of interior to get a permission to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So are you saying, as we need to clarify this for ourselves, are you saying that the SJBs were no longer reporting at all whatsoever to the CSB because of these town commands? Is that what you are asserting for us?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm not saying that. That's your conclusion, and it's a wrong conclusion. I'm presenting you facts, and I never said that the employees of the public security service did not report. What I said was that the town commanders did not have to ask for an approval in relation to involvement of police forces in the territory. The town commander could have simply said, all of you authorised officials as well as reserve police members are going to the front line in Jajce, without having to justify this to anyone except to the Crisis Staff, and the Crisis Staff, when you think about how these were organised, they would then explain the situation to the military commands, political organs, and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you tell us within the Bosanska Krajina which municipalities had these town commands? Just list them for us.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I wouldn't say many, but I can tell you about one, and that's Kljuc. Now, if you are asking me whether there was one in Prijedor, I don't recall at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I think it was misinterpreted, 27/15. I believe the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Something different.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We have recorded here that you said you wouldn't say many of the municipalities had town commands and then you recall one which is Kljuc, is that a correct description of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It is correct, but I must add that we did not deal with town commands or we didn't monitor them, so I'm saying there is a possibility that town commands existed in some other municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I have four minutes so I want to show you one more document.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: It's P703.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, on Monday you testified about your efforts to arrange for exhumations of the victims of the Mice group. First of all, in the upper right-hand corner it says "Zupljanin - opinion," can you tell us whose handwriting that is?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can only assume. I do believe I'm right there. This is the handwriting of Nedeljko Kesic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You write in this letter: "In the interest of a proper investigation and presentation of the truth, it is essential you form a forensic team consisting, if possible, of military medical examiners from Belgrade who would come to Teslic as quickly as possible." So are you asking Mr. Zupljanin to actually form this forensic team? Is that what you are asking?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This should be understood as a request for assistance since I am -- I was a lawyer, I knew who was in charge of establishing such teams and who is authorised to do so. So this is exclusively under the jurisdiction of the prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, if you look up a little -- up in the letter, you said there was an agreement between representatives of the army, the president, and lower court, president of the lower court and the public prosecutor, and based on that agreement, it was decided that exhumation should be conducted; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it is, but let me repeat this. I asked rather than requested assistance because I knew that in the area of Teslic or Doboj there aren't available experts, mobile teams, that could conduct exhumation of two, according to the information we had, rather big mass graves. And that's the reason why we are urging Belgrade to provide us some assistance because we knew that there is a person with great authority, Professor Dr. Zoran Stankovic. I think his name is Stankovic. He later became a general, he was a military medicine forensic expert and head of the hospital, military academy hospital in Belgrade, and we believed that if we could involve him, we would make sure that the job is done quickly and well.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could we after the break clarify the confusion about the P number of OTP's document under tab number 33, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your permission since I'm under oath, I would like to complete yesterday's answer of mine -- actually both the question and the answer were not complete and it concerns a question put to me by Mr. Krgovic. He asked me whether it was possible for someone to provide the Milos group with false information without their knowledge, and I did not want to expand on this answer, but I would like to add one sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Radulovic, just give me a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This seems like evidence, and, of course this is at the close of evidence. Unless there is a question, I'm not sure he should comment on answers he gave to Mr. Krgovic or anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I didn't understand him to be commenting on it, he asked to be able to complete his answer, and having heard him, if it's a matter in which Mr. Krgovic, first of all, has a follow-up question, he will be permitted to do so, then, of course, you will be permitted to ask any consequencial question in re-examination. Yes, Mr. Radulovic, please summarise what you are starting to explain.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, Your Honours, I want to thank you for permitting me to complete my answer. So after the operation in Teslic, a whole avalanche of accusations came in relation to myself, Mr. Zupljanin, and all of those who were involved in arresting Mices. This could be seen in the media at meetings of political leadership, and the claim was that Stojan Zupljanin was trying to get more authority by getting control over certain police stations and municipal centres. They used all sorts of misinformation involving some private issues, issues that did not involve only myself but also my family. The same applied to Stojan and other people who participated in the operation. Attempts were made to present in the media the death of Stefan Markovic and Colonel Stevilovic, who was not an accident, and many other things were being mentioned which were silly. Among other things, they claimed I was born in 1943, that I was a war orphan, that I was born in Konjevic Polje, that I come from an undefined family, and that my -- and I was assigned with a task of killing Serbs. To show you that this is not something innocuous, I want to say that Dzevad Galijasevic provided the very same information in a book he published. This book is testimony to the fact that I have not tried to cover up anything here in my testimony before this court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. We will take the break now and during the break, Mr. Krgovic would decide whether he needs to ask a question arising out of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I can tell you now, I don't have further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. And, Mr. Olmsted, as I said, if you could decide during the break whether it is necessary for you to ask a question arising out of what the witness has just volunteered.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Just so that if he is done he is done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The Bench has --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Okay, I'll wait.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, with your kind permission and our apology and excuse, Mr. Krgovic and I we have a plane to catch, we are going on a mission this afternoon, so we will be -- we are required to leave at 11.30 so I just wanted to inform the Trial Chamber that we will rise at 11.30 and leave. I'm really sorry for this, but we anticipated that this would be over by now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I don't have a plane to catch but I know that Mr. Hannis wants to occupy my seat, so I will leave after this witness is completed as well, if that's all right. And to Judge Delvoie's question, tab 33 is 65 ter 2837 which was admitted as P1388. And the Prosecution has no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Radulovic, the Trial Chamber has a few questions of you before your testimony is finally brought to an end. Judge Delvoie.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Radulovic, we have information that the resubordination of police forces only applied for front-line assignments. You said something similar in your testimony this morning as an example of what the town command could do -- you said, just one moment, the town command could have simply said, all of you authorised officials as well as reserve police members are going to the front-line. My question is, do you confirm or do you deny that this authority over the police force by the town command was only for front-line assignments, or could they, for instance, give orders in regard to traffic regulation or crime prevention?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Everything that had to do with the municipal territory in which the town command was operational, it could deploy everybody in the zone that was under the command of the town. All the activities it dealt with, you understood that correctly. This included the front lines to protect that part of the territory, they could be sent out for other activities. The chief of the police station, as he was referred to then, was subordinated to the commander of the town defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. And there where the town command existed, was that -- was that a part of the Crisis Staff, was it a subgroup, so to speak, of a few persons of the Crisis Staff, or was it something out of and independent of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It wasn't independent of the Crisis Staff. It was under the control of the Crisis Staff. It was a separate group of people, separate by their professional and other skills, who were doing tasks that had to do with the armed resistance, the defence. It was a legal organ established as such and every municipality had the option of having a town command as well as a Crisis Staff, if they wished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. And then at a certain moment in time, Crisis Staffs were replaced by War Staffs or war commissions or whatever their name was. My question is, there were at that moment were town commands, what was the fate of those town commands then? What happened to the town commands when Crisis Staffs were replaced by War Staffs?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can say only what I know, I know that for a relatively brief period of time, these town commands existed, relatively briefly, and then what happened was that the army or rather, the 1st Krajina Corps subordinated all the armed formations under its control except for formations that were linked to the Ministry of Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And then a last question. You said that the town command had authority on all armed forces on the territory, police forces, army forces. Does that include para-military forces as well?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is a logical question, but the term para-military formation itself means that they were not under anybody's control. These were renegade units or groups that were not controlled by the army or by the police. Unfortunately in some areas they were quite strong and organised, and they committed atrocious crimes. When I say atrocious, I'm thinking of war crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Radulovic, just to follow up on one of your answers to Judge Delvoie. You told Judge Delvoie that the town commands only existed relatively briefly, and I was curious to know if you were able to give a rough indication of the time-period in which the town commands were effective in the municipalities where they were, in fact, established?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I would like to give you an answer, but I'm not able to be specific. I told you, I told the Trial Chamber that I had nothing to do with the town command. This was not my group's area of interest, the Milos group, but I know for sure that these town commands were not set up at the same time in all the areas of the municipality. As the complexity of the war situation evolved, the town commands would be set up in certain places and abolished. This is a feature of the period of May and June 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thanks. Then I had a question for you in relation to something which you told us Friday last when you were

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Special Police detachment in Banja Luka was, at a certain point in time, under the control of the Assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, and that it was the Assembly who decided to dispatch the Special Police force from Banja Luka to Doboj. Do you recall you giving testimony to this? Before you answer, my question is, if this is correct, whether the autonomous -- whether the Assembly of the ARK could dispose over the Special Police detachment without at least consulting with Stojan Zupljanin. Do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was shown that document for the first time here in the courtroom. This is not a document of the Milos group. And the document was shown to me by the Defence counsel asking me if this fact was known to me, just as you have asked me now. And I said that I'm seeing the document for the first time but I believe that it is authentic and I believe that the information that I got via the monitor about which my opinion was asked by the Defence counsel is accurate, so this is not information that is mine regarding the special detachment, the autonomous region, and the organisation and the decisions that were adopted by that Assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, your answer is that you really don't know if the Assembly of the ARK was able to exert any control over the Special Police detachment; is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, yes, you understood me correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, I have no more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would just like to have your permission to ask two questions relating to questions put by His Honour Judge Delvoie about the defence of the town and also to show a document very briefly that has to do with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Comrade Radulovic, when you were answering these questions about the functioning of the town command you gave your answers on the basis of what you know, about what happened in the municipality of Kljuc; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And then you talked about them existing in other places but in a form more variant that you really couldn't speak about specifically; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADULOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show the witness Exhibit 65 ter 10368. Your Honours, this is something that we received yesterday from the Prosecutor. It was disclosed e-mailed to us. They planned to use it in the redirect, but I'm now going to use that document myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would object to this. We did disclose the document yesterday evening. We were researching the concept of town command. This doesn't arise out of Your Honour's questions and it's regarding a municipality that the witness has already said he didn't know anything about. I believe it's Donji Vakuf, and we don't even have an English translation in front of us, so I don't think this is an appropriate issue to cover at this stage in this witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, practically speaking, can we really go any farther with this?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just in response to my question in the cross-examination, he did refer to Donji Vakuf as one of the municipality, so this is one with the war command, the town command, so I wanted to put a question about that to the witness, but if the Trial Chamber believes that it is not necessary, then I will not go ahead and do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It's not appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: In as much as the witness is here, I could see why you wish to do it, but in practical terms, as I said, can we make any headway with this? Mr. Radulovic, we thank you for your testimony before the Tribunal and you would be relieved to hear me say that you are now released as a witness, and we wish you a safe journey back to your home. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And while the next witness is on his way in, counsel may withdraw as they indicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, sorry, there are some preliminary matters which perhaps we should deal with before the witness enters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. O'Sullivan. Could the usher hold the witness for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I believe there's some matters that we need to deal with in terms of the scope of the expert report and the scope of testimony, and I discussed this briefly with Mr. Hannis, and I don't know what his position is on -- precisely what his position is going to be on these matters. Does Mr. Hannis -- Your Honour, would Mr. Hannis want me to go first, or does he want to? Yes, all right. First in relation to the report on the 14th of August last year, the Prosecution filed its supplemental motion pursuant to Rule 94 bis which included the testimony of Riedlmayer. And I'm referring to -- in that submission I'm referring to the page stamped 3.205, and there the Prosecution indicates that the relevant paragraphs and counts of the indictment are count 1 and paragraph 26(i) in relation to Mr. Stanisic. That's 13 municipalities. And paragraph 27(i) in relation to Mr. Zupljanin, and that's six municipalities. In paragraph 26 and 27 of the indictment, we are referred to schedule E of the indictment which sets out the cultural property, and that's why I say there are 13 municipalities charged against Mr. Stanisic and six against Mr. Zupljanin. And the allegation is that the destruction occurred during 1992. The expert report of this witness is 65 ter 10367.02, and this -- a draft of that report was given to us on the 14th of August, 2009. Now, that draft report and the final report we've just received with the 65 ter number I've just given you, states that at paragraph 13 of the report Mr. Riedlmayer was asked to prepare a report covering the 13 municipalities in schedule E and one additional municipality, that being Belica, from schedule F. So our position is that the Prosecution may only rely on the expert report in relation to these 14 municipalities. We've received notice that the charges relate to the 14 municipalities I just brought your attention to and that you can only make findings in relation to those 14 municipalities. I raise this as a preliminary matter because you've seen from Mr. Riedlmayer's report that he has incorporated his work from previous trials and previous reports he has prepared, and the material is much more expansive. The material in the attachments to the annexes goes well beyond these 14 municipalities, and our position is, that the Prosecution should only be able to lead evidence in relation to those 14 municipalities and not the rest, and the Chamber cannot take any notice or make any findings in relation to any other municipality except those 14. That's the first matter I wish to raise. You are quite capable of separating the wheat from the chaff, I have no doubt about that, I'm just saying that if Mr. Riedlmayer has incorporated other research into his report, that's fine, but we are limited in this trial to schedule E and one municipality from schedule F. That's my first point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan, did you want to make your second, you said you had -- that was your first point. Did you want to address all of your concerns and have Mr. Hannis then respond or deal with them one at a time?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Those are my submissions in relation to the scope of his report. My second submission has to do with the scope of his expertise. We say that this witness can't provide opinion evidence in relation to the sites charged in the indictment, which I've just set out for you. He can say whether there is cultural property located at those sites, that's the first area that he can testify to, and he can say whether and to what extent there has been damage to those sites, we say that's his scope of his ability to give opinion evidence. He is a historian, a librarian, a bibliographer with knowledge concerning cultural property. We say he cannot give evidence regarding alleged perpetrators, and we say he cannot give evidence of whether and when any of the alleged damage occurred. We say those are matters that are not within his expertise. In addition -- under Rule 89(C) in addition to the fact that it's beyond his expertise, he cannot talk about perpetrators or when [indiscernible] occurred because we say he has no personal knowledge of those events, he only visited Bosnia after the war. His report sometimes makes reference to hearsay accounts or hearsay documents, we have no opportunity to cross-examine, of course, the makers of those hearsay accounts, and we refer you, once again, to the Appeals Chamber, jurisprudence in Alexovski [phoen], which we say gives guidance to a Trial Chamber on the admissibility of hearsay, and I refer you to paragraph 44 of Alexovski Appeals Chamber decision. That is IT-1995-14/1, AR 73, 16 February 1999. There the Appeals Chamber indicated that for a Trial Chamber to decide on Rule 89(C) you must consider the fact that the person who recorded the interviews, that's Mr. Riedlmayer himself, has no shared experience with the people who may or the documents which may have provided information to him. We cannot cross-examine on that material that he recorded, and the ability to cross-examine Mr. Riedlmayer on it, of course, does not assist the accused in the ability to confront the truth and accuracy of any of that information. You will recall that we've also brought to your attention the Milutinovic jurisprudence, that's IT-05-87T, two decisions one from the 1st of September, 2006 and one from the 8th of September, 2006, and the last jurisprudence, which we think might be the most on point by analogy at least, is the Appeals Chamber decision in Milosevic, IT-02-54, AR 73.2, the decision of the 30th of September, 2002, in relation to the admissibility of the evidence of an OTP investigator. Now, the facts in that case, the investigator had read witness statements. An investigator was proposed as a witness, the summarising witness, as they were referred to in those days, who was going to express his conclusions based on statements he had read by other people. Now, the primary statements were not admitted, and the maker of the primary statements were not called. The Trial Chamber upheld an appeal by the Appeals Chamber ruled that there was a sufficient indicia of reliability to those statements based on the application of the Alexovski Appeals Chamber jurisprudence. So, Your Honour, we say that the threshold question of admissibility has not been met. There's no indicia of reliability for you to allow Mr. Riedlmayer to testify in relation to alleged perpetrators or to the alleged dates of 1992. I might add that in all three of the decisions I mentioned, Milutinovic and Milosevic, the hearsay evidence was ruled inadmissible under 89(C). So to summarise, we say, as a matter of law and of common sense, that it's beyond the scope of this witness to speak about alleged perpetrators and whether or not the damage occurred in 1992, both in relation to his expertise and under Rule 89(C). Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, in addition to what my learned friend Mr. O'Sullivan just said, we absolutely adopt the position of Zupljanin Defence. First of all, Your Honours, with regard to the position -- we adopt position of Stanisic Defence. With regard to position of Zupljanin Defence, frankly, we don't see any reason to see and to hear this particular witness, Mr. Riedlmayer. In fact, he submitted photos of certain sites. He is speaking about the -- to some extent some background issues. Absolutely, of course, this is a theory of Prosecution case and they are absolutely free to lead their evidence and to create and tailor their part of the case, but our position is that this particular witness is absolutely -- he is not fitting in the judicial economy principles in the trial because his work is absolutely of no use for the experience fact-finders like you are. With that regard, I would like to make reference to the decision of Trial Chamber III in -- which was rendered of 14th of April this year. This is a case Prosecutor versus Seselj, case number IT-03-67T, and this decision is related to the admission of evidence presented during the testimony of Andras Riedlmayer. Inter alia, Trial Chamber in Seselj case found, and I'm quoting apart from paragraph 15 of the decision: "Nevertheless, the Chamber notes that on several occasions the expert went beyond his specific area of competence to comment on issues of admissibility attributing the destruction of monuments even the deaths of known Serbian civilians, to Serbian nationalist or even to Serb forces. The Chamber insists on the fact that an expert may not comment on issue of -- issues of responsibility. Consequently, the Chamber will not take into consideration the parts of the report which go beyond the expert's specific area of competence. Notably, those parts where he expresses his opinion on the responsibility of the perpetrators of the destruction of cultural and religious property with which he became familiar while compiling his report." So, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, isn't this just a repetition of what Mr. O'Sullivan has just raised, namely, that of course --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... this is -- I'd just like to point out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... on matters beyond his expertise --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... so in future, please, I mean, we will assess the evidence. Please disregard any part of Riedlmayer's report or any testimony with that regard. If you disregard these points, you will have nothing of his report, and this is useless to spend precious time here. That's my point. But let's see what our friends will say from Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I'll begin with Mr. Pantelic. If I understand what he's saying he is saying that this witness has no relevant evidence. If that's the case, then under Rule 94 bis regarding expert witnesses, paragraph B3 says a party is supposed to within 30 days of disclosure of the statement notify whether or not it challenges the qualifications of the witness as an expert or the relevance of all or parts of the statement and if so, which parts. He didn't do that until this very moment. And that's a general point I would make regarding Mr. O'Sullivan's bringing this up today before the witness comes on. It just works as a better matter for all of us, I think, if these things are raised in writing sufficiently in advance so that the parties can make intelligent submissions citing relevant authority and giving you sufficient time to consider that information and reach and informed decision with adequate time, rather than having to do it at the last minute. The same goes for the Prosecution, and I bear that in mind, we need to do that as well. Now, regarding Mr. O'Sullivan's submissions, I should say, I can save time for you. The Prosecution is not asking you to rely on what Mr. Riedlmayer has put in his database regarding observations about perpetrators. He does report hearsay statements from the Imam, from a local person he interviewed, from newspaper accounts where it may have been reported that this mosque was destroyed by Serb extremists or Serb forces or Serb soldiers, Serb police, we are not asking you to rely on that. We are going to have to prove that through other evidence. But -- and I think that makes sense given the nature of what has been destroyed and who the source of authority is, you might have some concerns about the motivation of that person regarding their account of who destroyed it. But we take a different position regarding when the destruction occurred, and I would ask Your Honours to consider that evidence. I don't think it should be inadmissible per se. Hearsay is admissible in this Tribunal, and we think that you might rely on that evidence, maybe not find it sufficient standing by itself, but of some evidence you can consider as to when the destruction occurred. Summer 1992, June 1992, whatever. And we would ask you to decide against Mr. O'Sullivan in terms of whether or not you can consider his report and the database entries regarding dates. Again, look at the source. Is it an unnamed individual, is it the local Imam, is it more than one source? Does it come from a Serb, a Muslim? Is it in a media account that was contemporaneous with the events? Those are factors we say you should consider in deciding whether or not to admit that evidence regarding the dates of the damage. And the first point that Mr. O'Sullivan raised was the scope of the report and going beyond the 14 municipalities, I think in schedule E the total number of sites we have listed is something in the neighbourhood of 112. And with the exception of one site listed in the indictment, Mr. Riedlmayer has photographs or entries in the database concerning all of those. The only one for which there is no photograph or report is regarding Vlasenica and the Drum mosque. We have no photo or information about that and the Prosecution will be withdrawing that one. But we say you should be able to consider the total database because in the indictment, part of the allegation against these accuseds, paragraph 40, it talks about the restrictive and discriminatory measures on the Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Croat population and then alleges that the Bosnian Serb forces and their leadership engaged in a campaign of terror designed to drive them out of the country. We say this, what we see as widespread and systematic destruction of the religious and cultural sites, was part of that campaign of terror designed to make life unbearable and force people, non-Serb people to leave. Paragraph 42 of the indictment is a general allegation that says, all acts and omissions charged as crimes against humanity were part of a widespread or systematic attack directed against the Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Croat civil population of Bosnia-Herzegovina.
